issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette:
Ravi, a 53-year-old painter, had been working on a mural in a public square when a mortar shell struck a nearby market. The blast threw him off his ladder; he landed on his side, his body twisted, as smoke and dust filled the air. In the months that followed, the smell of burnt fabric or any sharp bang-a car backfiring, a door slamming-would send his heart racing and his muscles tensing, his body bracing for danger. To Ravi, each sharp bang or burning smell instantly confirmed that danger was everywhere, and he would think, "This is what the world is now." This conviction that the world was dangerous kept pulling him back to the memory of the explosion itself, feeding it, making it more vivid-he wasn't just recalling the blast, he was there again, and the danger felt absolute. Those same triggers would also drag him back into the memory: his limbs would lock into that same twisted position, and he would be overwhelmed by a wave of grief for the people he had seen injured. Each time, the memory felt so extreme that it seemed unreal, and he would think, "The world is a dangerous place-there is no safety anywhere." These thoughts made him feel that nothing in his life mattered anymore, and that he was no longer capable of the work that had defined him.

Believing he was no longer the man he had been, Ravi began to avoid news reports about the conflict, certain that seeing them would only confirm his loss. He also started to keep himself busy at all hours, taking on extra painting jobs he did not need, because idleness brought the unbearable question of why this had happened to him. His conviction that the world was dangerous made him interpret every unfamiliar smell or sudden sound as a potential threat, scanning his environment for signs of trouble even in his own backyard. When he did remember the event, his negative appraisals colored the recollection: the grief felt even heavier because he believed he should have been able to help, and the unreal quality of the memory made him doubt his own mind.

The memory itself intruded without warning-his body would reenact the fall, and the accompanying grief would feel as fresh as the day it happened. In response, he would mentally go over the event again and again, searching for a reason why he had been singled out, and this rumination only made the memory more vivid and more frequent. Recalling the explosion also kept his body on high alert; he would lie in bed at night, tense and watchful, listening for sounds that might signal danger. Each intrusion reinforced his belief that he could no longer handle the ordinary demands of his life, deepening his sense of futility.

Living in a state of constant hypervigilance-his body always ready to react-Ravi found himself jumping at ordinary sounds like a neighbor closing a car door. The persistent sense of threat kept the explosion close in his mind, and the memory would surface without a trigger, as if the adrenaline itself called it up. This hypervigilance, in turn, made him more likely to notice potential triggers; a faint smell of smoke while cooking would immediately pull him into a memory of the blast. The threat he felt also drove him to keep busy, because slowing down meant confronting the fear that was always simmering beneath the surface. And his vigilance confirmed his appraisal that the world was dangerous: if he had to be this watchful, danger must be real.

Yet his efforts to manage only deepened the cycle. Keeping busy meant he spent long hours in his studio, where the smell of paint thinner-reminiscent of the dust and chemical odors from the blast-became an unavoidable trigger. Ruminating about why the event happened to him kept the memory alive, and avoiding the news left him unprepared for the occasional headline he could not escape, which would spike his anxiety. His constant busyness also left him exhausted, yet he could not stop, because stopping made him feel the tension in his body even more acutely.

Six months after the bombing, Ravi's wife insisted he see a doctor. He came to the clinic not because he believed therapy could help, but because he was tired of living with a body that never relaxed and a mind that would not stop circling back to that single moment. What frightened him most was the thought that he might never feel capable again-that the man who had once painted with confidence was gone for good.

violations.explanation: No paragraph conveys that triggers directly lead to negative appraisals; triggers lead to memory which then leads to appraisals.
No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly leads to intrusive memory; threat leads to hypervigilance and triggers, but not directly to memory.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph conveys that triggers directly lead to negative appraisals; triggers lead to memory which then leads to appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Threat → Memory: No paragraph conveys that the sense of threat directly leads to intrusive memory; threat leads to hypervigilance and triggers, but not directly to memory.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
